Background Target condition being diagnosed Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is a blood‐borne virus causing liver inflammation, and if untreated, it can seriously damage the liver ( EASL 2020 ; WHO 2024 ). Around the world, 58 million people are living with chronic HCV infection, and about 1.5 million new infections occur each year ( WHO 2024 ). Hepatitis C is diagnosed by applying a serological test to identify people infected with the virus. In the case of a positive test, a nucleic acid test for HCV ribonucleic acid (RNA) is needed to confirm the infection ( EASL 2020 ; WHO 2018 ). Hepatitis C is often asymptomatic until symptoms or manifestations of chronic liver disease occur ( EASL 2020 ; WHO 2024 ). About 30% of people with HCV will clear the infection spontaneously from their bodies and will not need treatment ( WHO 2024 ). Chronic damage to the liver occurs in 55% to 85% of infected people ( WHO 2024 ). WHO reported 290,000 HCV deaths in 2019, primarily due to cirrhosis (advanced stage of fibrosis) and primary liver cancer ( WHO 2024 ). It takes a long time to develop cirrhosis, and the risk of developing cirrhosis within the next 20 years in people with HCV varies between 15% and 30% ( WHO 2024 ). Meta‐analysis of histological data in the viral hepatitis (METAVIR) scoring system is the current standard for assessing liver fibrosis ( METAVIR 1996 ). Translation of different fibrosis staging systems to METAVIR can be found in Table 1 . Liver biopsy, non‐invasive tests, and imaging techniques are all used to assess the degree of liver damage. The stages of liver fibrosis are defined according to the METAVIR histopathological scoring system, where F0 is defined as 'absence of fibrosis'; F1 is defined as 'mild fibrosis'; F2 is defined as 'significant fibrosis'; F3 is defined as 'severe fibrosis'; and F4 is defined as 'cirrhosis' ( METAVIR 1996 ). The degree of liver damage (stage of fibrosis) defines the treatment, prognosis, and clinical outcomes in a person with chronic HCV infection ( AASLD‐IDSA 2021 ; Everhart 2010 ). 1 Translation of different fibrosis (F) staging systems to METAVIR Classification of the target conditions Stage of estimated fibrosis According to the prioritised for treatment According to the high risk for developing complications METAVIR ( French METAVIR Cooperative Study Group 1994 ) Ishak ( Ishak 1995 ) Knodell ( Knodell 1981 ) Scheuer ( Scheuer 1991 ) Kleiner ( Kleiner 2005 ) No significant fibrosis No advanced fibrosis F0 – No fibrosis F0 – No fibrosis F0 – No fibrosis F0 – No fibrosis F0 – No fibrosis F1 – Mild fibrosis Portal fibrosis without septa F1 – Minimal fibrosis F1 – Portal fibrosis F1 – enlarged fibrotic portal tracts F1 ‐ Perisinusoidal or periportal ‐ 1; Mild, zone 3, perisinusoidal ‐ 1A, Moderate, zone 3, perisinusoidal ‐ 1B, Portal/periportal ‐ 1C fibrosis At least significant fibrosis F2 – Moderate fibrosis Portal fibrosis with few septa F2 – Mild fibrosis F2 – Periportal fibrosis F2 ‐ Periportal or portal‐portal septa but intact architecture F2 ‐ Perisinusoidal and portal/periportal fibrosis At least advanced fibrosis F3 – Severe fibrosis Numerous septa without cirrhosis F3 – Moderate fibrosis F4 – Moderate‐severe fibrosis F3 – Septal fibrosis F3 – fibrosis with architectural distortion F3 ‐ Bridging fibrosis F4 – Cirrhosis F5 – Severe fibrosis and incomplete cirrhosis F6 – Probable / definite cirrhosis F4 ‐ Cirrhosis F4 – probable or define cirrhosis F4 ‐ Cirrhosis Clinically significant fibrosis is generally defined as F2 or worse. In this review, based on the clinical implications of distinguishing between the different stages of fibrosis, we have considered the three target conditions below as defined by the METAVIR score (see Table 1 ). At least significant fibrosis (stages F2‐F4) compared to no significant fibrosis (stages F0‐F1), as this group is prioritised for treatment ( EASL 2020 ). At least advanced fibrosis (stages F3‐F4) compared to no advanced fibrosis (stages F0‐F2), as this group is at high risk of developing complications, i.e. hepatocellular carcinoma ( EASL 2020 ). Cirrhosis (stage F4) compared with no cirrhosis (stages F0‐F3) because the duration and effectiveness of treatment in these groups are different ( EASL 2020 ). Index test(s) The index test in our review is the aspartate aminotransferase‐to‐platelet ratio index (APRI). APRI is a non‐invasive test and can be calculated easily, using the formula: [(AST (aspartate aminotransferase)/upper limit of the normal AST range) X 100]/platelet count ( Wai 2003 ). This test was developed in 2003 as a non‐invasive alternative to liver biopsies ( Wai 2003 ). Studies followed, suggesting that APRI could be used to assess HCV‐related fibrosis ( Castera 2010 ; EASL 2020 ; Sebastiani 2009 ; Wai 2003 ; WHO 2018 ). The two variables included in the APRI formula should be routinely measured in primary care as part of the liver blood test, so APRI incurs no additional costs ( EASL 2021 ). APRI is an alternative to complex and costly non‐invasive machine‐based tests (Fibroscan, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computerised tomography (CT)). The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends the use of APRI for the diagnosis of advanced fibrosis in people with hepatitis C when liver biopsy or elastography is difficult to apply ( WHO 2018 ). There is no consensus on the thresholds for diagnosing different stages of fibrosis using APRI. The cut‐off for significant fibrosis (METAVIR F2‐F4) varies in the literature. A review by Lin and colleagues suggests an APRI cut‐off of 0.7 for diagnosing significant fibrosis ( Lin 2011 ). In a systematic review of blood tests for the diagnosis of fibrosis, Chou and colleagues identified four different APRI cut‐off ranges for diagnosing significant fibrosis: ≥ 0.5, > 0.55, > 1.5, and ≥ 1.5. Two cut‐off values were found (1.0 and 2.0) as thresholds for the diagnosis of cirrhosis ( Chou 2013 ). The European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL) has no recommendations about the cut‐off values that should be used in clinical practice ( EASL 2020 ). Liver biopsy and APRI should ideally be performed on the same day or within a short period (three months or less) as fibrosis is a dynamic process that may reverse if treatment is initiated or progress further if left untreated ( Butt 2015 ; Marcellin 2002 ; Morgan 2010 ; Zeremski 2016 ). Clinical pathway During the last decade, people with chronic HCV infection have been treated with direct‐acting antivirals (DAA) ( EASL 2020 ). The stage of fibrosis influences the duration of treatment with DAAs, and the stage of fibrosis is prognostic of the probability of sustained virological response (SVR) ( EASL 2020 ). The clinical pathway for the use of tests in screening and diagnosis of fibrosis and cirrhosis in people with chronic HCV infection (see Figure 1 ). 1 As a first step, liver fibrosis should be assessed in all people in whom HCV antibodies are found ( EASL 2020 ; WHO 2018 ). All people diagnosed with chronic HCV infection should be considered for treatment ( EASL 2020 ). Evaluation of liver fibrosis can be done using non‐invasive methods such as serological tests (routine blood tests, APRI, FIB‐4, serum markers, panels) or machine‐based technologies (transient elastography, ultrasound), or both ( AASLD‐IDSA 2021 ). Serological and machine‐based tests are less expensive than liver biopsies, are less time‐consuming, and carry no risk. A combination of non‐invasive tests can be used in order to increase accuracy ( AASLD‐IDSA 2021 ; EASL 2020 ). Liver biopsy is used when the results of two non‐invasive tests are discordant and the clinical diagnosis is unclear ( AASLD‐IDSA 2021 ). Liver biopsy also remains an option for patients with HCV infection in the presence of other chronic liver disease aetiologies, like metabolic syndrome, alcoholism, or autoimmunity ( EASL 2020 ). Non‐invasive evaluation of advanced fibrosis is recommended for making decisions regarding HCV treatment strategy and management of cirrhosis ( AASLD‐IDSA 2021 ). People with advanced fibrosis or with cirrhosis should remain under surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma and other complications like bleeding, infection, or ascites ( EASL 2020 ). The downstream consequences of testing include the following. True positive (TP): people would benefit from rapid diagnosis and referral to effective treatment. True negative (TN): people would be spared unnecessary treatment and would benefit from reassurance and the pursuit of an alternative diagnosis. False positive (FP): people would probably experience anxiety and morbidity caused by additional testing, unnecessary treatment, and possible adverse events, and the chance that a FP result may halt further diagnostic evaluation. False negative (FN): increased risk of morbidity and mortality, delayed treatment initiation, and lifestyle modifications. Prior test(s) Quantitative polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for HCV RNA is recommended for verification of HCV infection ( AASLD‐IDSA 2021 ). For diagnosis of chronic HCV infection, the PCR test for HCV RNA should be positive for six months or more. Once chronic HCV infection is diagnosed, the stage of fibrosis must be assessed. APRI can be one of the tests that people should undergo after the diagnosis of chronic hepatitis C for staging of fibrosis. Role of index test(s) APRI can be used as a triage or replacement test for liver biopsies. In clinical settings with adequate resources, APRI is usually used as a screening test in people with chronic hepatitis C. If APRI is positive, further confirmation with preferably non‐invasive tests such as transient elastography, or the invasive liver biopsy test, should be performed to confirm the diagnosis. APRI can be used as a replacement for liver biopsy for staging fibrosis in countries with inadequate resources ( EASL 2020 ). APRI can be used as a single test or in combination with other non‐invasive tests, in order to provide greater accuracy ( EASL 2020 ). However, in this review, we plan to evaluate the diagnostic test accuracy of APRI as a single test. Alternative test(s) Serum markers Several serum markers or a combination of them have been proposed as indicators of fibrosis. Serum markers reflect the process of necroinflammation followed by fibrosis in the liver parenchyma. The AST/alanine transaminase (ALT) ratio and the FIB‐4 are easy to use and, like APRI, are not patent‐protected ( Castera 2009 ). The FibroTest in Europe or FibroSure in the USA, the Fibrometers , FibroSpect II , the ELF (Enhanced Liver Fibrosis Test), Forn's index , and the Hepascore (PathWest, University of Western Australia, Australia) are commercially protected formulas which make them expensive to use ( Castera 2009 ). Imaging modalities Transient elastography, performed with Fibroscan ® equipment (Echosens, Paris, France), is used to assess the degree of fibrosis by measuring liver stiffness. Two‐dimensional shear wave elastography (2D‐SWE) using Aixplorer equipment is another technology for the detection of cirrhosis ( Herrmann 2018 ). CT, which uses computer‐generated radio waves, and MRI, which uses magnetic fields, can also be used to stage fibrosis and to diagnose cirrhosis, but because of their high cost, CT and MRI are less often used in clinical practice ( Yoshiji 2021 ). In clinical practice, the choice between machine‐based or serum marker methods is based on their availability and cost ( WHO 2018 ). Alternative tests will not be considered in this systematic review. Rationale Staging of fibrosis in people with chronic hepatitis C infection is essential for choosing the treatment and surveillance strategy ( AASLD‐IDSA 2021 ; EASL 2020 ). International guidelines recommend the use of non‐invasive methods for screening and diagnosis before treatment ( AASLD‐IDSA 2021 ; EASL 2021 ; WHO 2018 ). Simple scores based on blood tests such as APRI could be used for the diagnosis of fibrosis stage in countries with inadequate resources ( EASL 2020 ; WHO 2018 ). While APRI has no complications, no sampling errors (as opposed to liver biopsy in focal fibrosis), and can be used for staging of fibrosis, false negative results produced by the APRI test can lead to underestimation of the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma ( AASLD‐IDSA 2021 ). There are no clear recommendations regarding the use of APRI in assessing fibrosis and cirrhosis in people with chronic hepatitis C infection. The huge number of different non‐invasive tests and the lack of consensus about their use make the clinical choice difficult ( EASL 2021 ). Fibrogenesis is a dynamic process, and the first time fibrosis is detected typically occurs during the evolution of a disease or at the time of its diagnosis. Therefore, screening people for fibrosis, assessing the fibrosis stage, and identifying those in need of treatment to stop or reverse the fibrosis stage, or to remain under surveillance, should be imperative to prevent the further evolution of cirrhosis and the likely development of hepatocellular carcinoma. This is also why we use both concepts in our protocol. We found six reviews that have determined the diagnostic accuracy of APRI for the staging of fibrosis in adults with chronic HCV, using liver biopsy as the reference standard ( Chou 2013 ; El Serafy 2017 ; Houot 2016 ; Lin 2011 ; Patel 2025 ; Shaheen 2007 ). The review by Lin and colleagues ( Lin 2011 ) was an update of the review by Shaheen and colleagues ( Shaheen 2007 ). The review published by El Serafy and colleagues included studies assessing APRI only in people from Egypt having chronic HCV infection ( El Serafy 2017 ). The latest review was published in support of the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) Guideline and included studies through to April 2022 ( Patel 2025 ). All these reviews included approximately 85 studies with approximately 18,000 participants with chronic HCV infection. We evaluated these reviews according to AMSTAR 2 ( Shea 2017 ) and found some disadvantages, such as lack of justification for the inclusion of studies with different types of study designs, lack of reasons for exclusion of studies, inadequate considerations of risk of bias in the meta‐analysed results, language and database limitations in searching for relevant literature, and heterogeneity being explored. We also found about 20 new articles that can be included in the analysis of our prospective review, and, alongside the use of Cochrane methodology, our review may change the conclusions of previously published reviews ( Garner 2016 ). Objectives To determine the diagnostic accuracy of the aspartate aminotransferase‐to‐platelet ratio index (APRI) for staging and screening fibrosis in adults with chronic hepatitis C infection when compared with liver biopsy as the reference standard. To achieve this, we will compare at least significant fibrosis (stages F2‐F4) to no significant fibrosis (stages F0‐F1) as this group of people is prioritised for treatment; at least advanced fibrosis (stages F3‐F4) compared to no advanced fibrosis (stages F0‐F2) as this group of people is at high risk for developing complications, i.e. hepatocellular carcinoma; cirrhosis (stage F4) compared to no cirrhosis (stages F0‐F3) as the duration and effectiveness of treatment in these population groups of people are different. Secondary objectives We also aim to identify the pooled sensitivity and specificity of the most common cut‐off values of APRI for the staging of fibrosis in adults with chronic hepatitis C. We plan to investigate heterogeneity for the following covariates if adequate data are available ( Investigations of heterogeneity ). Methodological quality: a) studies with high methodological quality; b) studies with low or unclear methodological quality Interval of liver biopsy and APRI: a) done in one day; b) more than one day, but less than or equal to three months Mean length of biopsy samples: a) less than 15 mm; b) mean length equal to or more than 15 mm Number of portal tracts in a biopsy sample: a) less than 11; b) number of portal tracts equal to or more than 11. Methods Criteria for considering studies for this review Types of studies We will include studies with a cross‐sectional design that report the TP, FP, FN, TN data, or other parameters that provide the information necessary to calculate the TP, FP, FN, and TN, in study participants with chronic HCV infection alone, with the use of APRI as index test and liver biopsy as reference standard, irrespective of language, year, or publication status, or whether data were collected prospectively or retrospectively. We will include studies published as abstracts, poster presentations, or in letter form (identified as described in Electronic searches and Searching other resources ), if we obtain the data needed for analysis. We will include studies in which the median time interval between the index test and the reference standard is three months or less. If the median time interval between the index test and biopsy is not reported or cannot be obtained from the study authors, we will exclude the study. If the APRI is used for screening, a FN will be detected on biopsy because we will exclude studies using different reference standards that do not include a liver biopsy.  We will exclude case‐control studies that compare people with known fibrosis stages to matched controls due to the high risk of bias in such studies ( Whiting 2011 ) (see Appendix 1 ). If we find randomised clinical trials that compare APRI with other index tests, we will consider for inclusion the APRI arm. Participants Inclusion criteria We will include studies, irrespective of country of origin, with participants at least 18 years old, of any sex, gender, and ethnicity, with a confirmed diagnosis of chronic HCV infection. We will include participants regardless of whether they are treatment‐naive or have received previous treatment. Exclusion criteria We will exclude studies that included participants with chronic hepatitis C and co‐infections (human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) or hepatitis B virus (HBV)), alcohol abuse, or any of these combinations. The reason for our choice is that the APRI score is only validated for use in people with chronic hepatitis C infection ( Wai 2003 ). However, if these studies reported data separately for participants with chronic HCV infection without alcohol abuse or co‐infection with HIV or HBV, then, in our analyses, we will include data from such participants alone. We will also exclude studies that do not report the required data for performing the analyses and if we cannot obtain the missing data from study authors. However, we will list such studies in 'Excluded studies' and provide the reasons for their exclusion. Index tests The index test is APRI. As provided in the Index test(s) section of the Background, for the calculation of the APRI index test score, we will use the formula [(AST/upper limit of the normal AST range) X 100]/platelet count or online calculators like AST to Platelet Ratio Index (APRI) Calculator - Clinical Calculators - Hepatitis C Online (uw.edu) or AST to Platelet Ratio Index (APRI) - MDCalc. We will need data on the amount of AST (IU/L), the upper limit of the normal AST (IU/L), and the platelet count in the body (x 10 9 /L). Although there may be variations in the concentration of markers in different blood samples, this should not result in significant changes in the test results ( Giannini 2005 ). Target conditions METAVIR defines five stages of fibrosis ( METAVIR 1996 ); i.e. F0, defined as absence of fibrosis (i.e. no fibrosis or little fibrosis); F1, defined as mild fibrosis (i.e. portal fibrosis without septa); F2, defined as significant fibrosis (i.e. thin fibrous septa emanating from portal triads); F3, defined as severe fibrosis (i.e. fibrous septa bridging portal triads and central veins); and F4, defined as cirrhosis. So, based on METAVIR, we define fibrosis and cirrhosis (our target conditions) in people with chronic hepatitis C as below. At least significant fibrosis (stages F2‐F4) compared with no significant fibrosis (stages F0‐F1) because people with significant fibrosis should be treated ( EASL 2020 ). At least advanced fibrosis (stages F3‐F4) compared with no advanced fibrosis (stages F0‐F2) because people with advanced fibrosis are at high risk of developing complications, i.e. hepatocellular carcinoma ( EASL 2020 ). Cirrhosis (stage F4) compared with no cirrhosis (stages F0‐F3) as the duration and effectiveness of treatment in people with cirrhosis vary ( EASL 2020 ). Advanced fibrosis is the presence of fibrous septa bridging portal triads and central veins according to biopsy, which corresponds to F3 METAVIR score. Significant fibrosis corresponds to the F2‐F4 METAVIR scores. If the fibrosis stage has been evaluated with different semi‐quantitative morphological scales, we will convert the results to METAVIR score ( Table 1 ). Reference standards Liver biopsy is the reference standard for staging fibrosis in people with chronic HCV infection ( Rockey 2009 ). It should be obtained by percutaneous needle techniques, the transjugular method, or surgically obtained specimens of liver tissue for diagnosing fibrosis ( Rockey 2009 ). The criteria for an adequate specimen are a length of at least 15 mm and at least 11 portal tracts ( Rockey 2009 ). Liver histology is an imperfect reference standard due to its limitations ‐ a consequence of sample error and not being absolutely repeatable ( Regev 2002 ). The diagnosis and scoring of liver biopsy can be performed by various scoring systems. In the METAVIR system, significant fibrosis is graded on a scale of 2 to 4 ( Table 1 ). Stage 2: enlargement of the portal tract with rare septa formation Stage 3: numerous septa without cirrhosis Stage 4: cirrhosis. The time interval between the liver biopsy and the APRI test should be three months or less. We have chosen this interval as the target condition can change over time. Our scoping search indicated that there are many studies that would meet the strict eligibility criteria. For e.g., in five studies, liver biopsy and APRI were done on the same day, and four studies used an interval of less than three months. Search methods for identification of studies We will combine electronic searches with reading references of identified studies of possible interest. To minimise bias in our search results, we have followed the guidance in Chapter 6 of the Cochrane Handbook for Diagnostic Test of Accuracy Reviews ( Spijker 2023 ) and in PRISMA‐S ( Rethlefsen 2021 ) to plan and describe the search process for the review. Electronic searches The Cochrane Hepato‐Biliary Group (CHBG) Controlled Trials Register and the Cochrane Hepato‐Biliary Group Diagnostic Test of Accuracy Studies Register will be searched internally by the CHBG Information Specialist via the Cochrane Register of Studies Web. We will also search the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE ALL Ovid, Embase Ovid (Excerpta Medica Database), LILACS (VHL Regional Portal), Science Citation Index Expanded, and Conference Proceedings Citation Index ‐ Science. The latter two will be searched simultaneously through the Web of Science. Appendix 2 provides the search strategies for the respective databases, with the expected date range of the searches. We will provide the actual date of the electronic searches at the review stage. Searching other resources We will search online trial registries such as ClinicalTrial.gov (clinicaltrials.gov/), WHO International Clinical Trial Registry Platform ( www.who.int/ictrp ), EU Clinical Trials Register ( www.clinicaltrialsregister.eu/ ), The ISRCTN registry ( www.isrctn.com/ ), European Medicines Agency ( www.ema.europa.eu/ema/ ), Food and Drug Administration ( www.fda.gov ), as well as pharmaceutical company sources for ongoing studies and for study information. We will search grey literature sources such as reports, dissertations, theses, and conference abstracts (e.g. in Google Scholar), to identify further studies of interest for inclusion in our review. We will use the PubMed/MEDLINE “similar articles search” tool on all included studies. We will manually check citations and reference lists of the included studies, as well as any relevant systematic reviews identified. We will search for and examine any relevant retraction statements and errata for information through the Retraction Watch Database (retractionwatch.com/retraction-watch-database-user-guide/) ( Lefebvre 2024 ). We will contact the authors of the studies that fulfil our inclusion criteria to obtain missing information relevant to our review. We will provide the current date of searching 'Other resources' at the review stage. We will use the items from the PRISMA‐S checklist that are relevant to our review, and we will also ensure that we have reported and documented our searches as advised (PRISMA-S Checklist; Rethlefsen 2021 ). Data collection and analysis We will follow the guidelines provided in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Diagnostic Test Accuracy ( DTA Handbook 2023 ). Selection of studies Four review authors (CP, ED, TT, AM) will work in pairs and independently select studies for inclusion using EndNote ( EndNote ). If duplicates are identified during title and abstract screening, all identified articles will be reviewed by two independent authors. During the selection process, the four authors will screen the titles and abstracts of all retrieved records, obtained through searching electronic and other resources, and we will code them as 'retrieve' (eligible or potentially eligible/unclear)/Yes or maybe or 'do not retrieve'/No… or similar. Records will then be checked for duplicate publications, and instances will be recorded. Authors will retrieve the full text of all relevant and potentially relevant records. Two review authors (ED, AM) will independently screen the full text of the publications to identify studies for inclusion. During this process, ED and AM will also identify and record the reasons for excluding ineligible studies. ED and AM will contact study investigators of the included studies to obtain missing information required for the performance of this review. Authors will resolve any disagreements through discussion among themselves or, if required, will consult a fifth author (TT, KSG, or CP). We will identify and collate multiple reports of the same study so that each study, rather than each record, is the unit of interest in the review. We will show the inclusion study selection process in the review graphically, with a PRISMA‐S flow diagram ( Page 2021a ; Page 2021b ). For screening non‐English‐language publications, we will utilise Google Translate (translate.google.com) to assist with eligibility assessment. If needed, we will seek translators through the CHBG to assist with assessing the eligibility of studies. Data extraction and management Two review authors (ED, AM) will extract data using a data extraction sheet piloted on three studies. A third review author (KG or TT) will check all data extraction. A fourth review author (CP) will serve as an arbitrator in cases of disagreements among the review authors who extracted or checked the information. We will extract the following data. General information: study origin, year and language of publication, study design Participants' characteristics: chronic HCV infection as defined by the authors of the individual studies considered for inclusion; age; males/females; ethnicity; cirrhosis (compensated or decompensated); laboratory data Sample size: number of participants meeting the inclusion criteria, and the total number of participants included and tested The time interval between the index test (APRI) and the reference standard (liver biopsy) Techniques used for liver biopsy Funding for the study. To provide data for our analyses, the studies must provide data that can help us calculate the TP, FP, TN, and FN diagnostic values of APRI for diagnosing the target condition, using a 2 x 2 table. We will enter the data into Review Manager ( RevMan 2025 ). If information on any of the TP, FP, TN, and FN diagnostic test values or results is missing and cannot be found in multiple publications of the main study, we will contact the authors of the included studies, if possible, to obtain the missing information. We will also contact the study authors to obtain any additional information that may be missing and help us with this review. If we do not have the data for the 2 x 2 table, we will exclude the study. Dealing with indeterminate data As APRI involves simple blood tests that include platelet count and AST in which technical failures are rare, indeterminate results are not expected. However, we will exclude the indeterminate results from the analysis. Assessment of methodological quality We will use the revised quality assessment tool for diagnostic accuracy studies (QUADAS‐2) to assess risk of bias in the included diagnostic test accuracy studies and the applicability of their results ( Whiting 2011 ). QUADAS‐2 is based on four quality domains: participant selection, index test, reference standard, and flow and timing. There are signalling questions for each domain, used to make judgements in terms of risk of bias. The answers to the signalling questions are 'yes', 'no', or 'unclear'. The first three domains are also judged in terms of concerns regarding applicability, and the answers can be 'low', 'high', or 'unclear'. Appendix 1 shows the signalling questions for our review subject and the criteria that we will use to assess the methodological quality of each study in our review. Regarding the 'flow and timing' domain, we will consider an interval of three months or less as the most appropriate interval between the reference standard test and the index test. Two review authors (ED, AM) will independently assess the risk of bias in each domain and the applicability of the results. They will provide quotes and comments to support each judgement for each domain. In the event of discrepancies and no agreement is reached, a third author (CP or TT) will serve as the arbitrator. If we judge a study as 'low' on all domains relating to bias or applicability, then our overall judgement for that study will be 'low risk of bias' or 'low concern regarding applicability'. If we judge a study as 'high' or 'unclear' in one or more domains relating to bias or applicability, then our overall judgement for that study will be at 'high risk of bias' or as having 'concerns regarding applicability'. The guidance to arrive at judgements for risk of bias in each study domain is provided in Appendix 1 . We will use tabular and graphical displays to summarise QUADAS‐2 assessments. Statistical analysis and data synthesis We will carry out the analyses following the recommendations in Chapter 10 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Diagnostic Test Accuracy ( Takwoingi 2023a ). We will use Review Manager ( RevMan 2025 ) and the SAS macro, MetaDAS, for analysis and plotting ( Takwoingi 2023b ). For each target condition (i.e. stages F2‐F4 versus stages F0‐F1, stages F3‐F4 versus stages F0‐F2, and stage F4 versus stages F0‐F3), we will build 2 x 2 tables of the APRI performance (TP, TN, FP, FN) for every primary study and the reported thresholds. We will calculate the sensitivity and specificity, with their 95% confidence intervals (CI), for each study, using the Wilson score with continuity correction. We will present this information in forest plots and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve plots. For the primary objective (the diagnostic performance of APRI for screening and diagnosis of different stages of fibrosis in adults with chronic hepatitis C), we will perform a bivariate meta‐analysis using MetaDAS macro, available for SAS statistical package (using samples of code provided in Takwoingi 2023b ). We anticipate the primary studies will use different cut‐off values to report the accuracy of the estimates. We will perform a bivariate analysis for each threshold. For the secondary objective of the investigation of heterogeneity, we will perform hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (HSROC) curve using the MetaDAS macro for SAS using similar codes to those provided in Takwoingi 2023b . We will include one covariate at a time and assume common variance across the different levels of the categorical variables (all five covariates in this review are categorical (see Investigations of heterogeneity ). We will use log‐likelihood to measure the model fit and the likelihood ratio test to compare fits between different models. One review author (OB) will do the statistical analyses. Investigations of heterogeneity We will attempt to investigate the sources of heterogeneity as follows. Studies judged to be of high methodological quality compared to studies of low or unclear methodological quality because methodological quality may influence results ( DTA Handbook 2023 ) (categorical covariate). Studies with liver biopsy and APRI done in one day versus with a maximum interval of more than one day, but less than or equal to three months between liver biopsy and APRI (categorical covariate) ( Reference standards ). Studies in which the mean length of biopsy samples is less than 15 mm (inadequate length) compared to studies in which the mean length of biopsy samples is equal to or more than 15 mm (adequate length) as there are disagreements between pathologists in the evaluation of the stage of fibrosis when the mean biopsy sample is less than 15 mm ( Rockey 2009 ) (categorical covariate). Studies in which the number of portal tracts in a liver biopsy sample is less than 11 (inadequate number of portal tracts) compared to studies in which the number of portal tracts is equal to or more than 11 (adequate number of portal tracts) as there are disagreements between pathologists in the evaluation of the stage of fibrosis when the number of portal tracts in a liver biopsy sample is less than 11 ( Rockey 2009 ) (categorical covariate). Studies with biopsy samples having a mean length greater than 15 mm but with the number of portal tracts less than 11 will be pooled into a separate group. This group will be analysed after the overall analysis. Sensitivity analyses We plan to assess the influence of risk of bias in the included studies on diagnostic accuracy by performing sensitivity analyses, from which we will exclude studies with the following characteristics from the bivariate analysis. Excluding studies judged to be at 'high risk of bias' (i.e. at least one domain of QUADAS‐2 is judged as 'at high risk of bias' or as 'at unclear risk of bias' (see Appendix 1 ) Excluding studies not published as full text. Summary of findings table and assessment of the certainty of the evidence As recommended by the GRADE Working Group, we will rate the certainty of evidence as high (will not downgrade), moderate (will downgrade one level), low (will downgrade two levels), or very low (will downgrade by three or more levels) based on the following domains: study design, risk of bias, indirectness, inconsistency, imprecision, publication bias ( Schünemann 2020a ; Schünemann 2020b ). Study design: no downgrading for cross‐sectional or cohort studies in patients with diagnostic uncertainty. Due to our inclusion criteria, we do not expect to downgrade evidence based on study design. Risk of bias: we will use our QUADAS‐2 assessments for the assessment of this domain. We will consider the impact of the different aspects of QUADAS‐2 on the test results to decide about not downgrading (low risk of bias in the participant selection, index test, reference standards, and flow and timing domains in most studies), downgrading one level (unclear risk of bias in participant selection, index test, reference standards, or flow and timing domains in most studies), or downgrading two levels (high risk of bias in participant selection, index test, reference standards, or flow and timing domains in most studies). For more details on the classification of risk of bias, see Appendix 1 . Indirectness: we will use our QUADAS‐2 assessments for the assessment of this domain. We will use the applicability concerns in the participant selection, index test and reference standards domains to decide about not downgrading (low applicability concerns in the participant selection, index test and reference standards in most studies), downgrading one level (unclear applicability concerns in the participant selection, index test and reference standards in most studies), or downgrading two levels (high applicability concerns in the participant selection, index test and reference standards in most studies). For more details on the classification of applicability concerns, see Appendix 1 . Inconsistency: we will look at the CIs and overlapping of studies on the forest plots. We will conduct prespecified analyses to investigate potential sources of heterogeneity and downgrade the evidence accordingly. Imprecision: we will assess imprecision based on the CIs of sensitivity and specificity estimates. As to the width of CIs, we will consider a 0.10 in sensitivity and 0.10 in specificity as clinically important. This is arbitrary and based on clinicians' preferences for one test over another, assuming a difference in sensitivity of 0.10 (with similar specificity) or vice versa. We will not downgrade for publication bias as there are no validated methods to assess the impact of publication in diagnostic accuracy studies. As the index test is based on routinely available laboratory tests, 'for profit' interest is unlikely to be a source of publication bias. However, study authors may choose not to report their results if they felt that the diagnostic accuracy of the test in their settings was lower than that reported in the literature. Because of the common nature of the tests that contribute to the index test, it is nearly impossible to assess whether study authors chose not to publish their results because of lower‐than‐expected diagnostic test accuracy. We will use GRADEpro GDT to prepare a summary of findings table for each of our target conditions. Participants with at least significant fibrosis (stages F2‐F4) versus participants with no significant fibrosis (stages F0‐F1). Participants with at least advanced fibrosis (stages F3‐F4) versus participants with no advanced fibrosis (stages F0‐F2). Participants with cirrhosis (stage F4) versus participants with no cirrhosis (stages F0‐F3). If the sensitivity analysis with study results at low risk of bias produces results that differ significantly from the main analyses, we will present the results of both analyses in the 'Results section' of the review. We will also discuss the robustness of our findings and utilise the results when drawing conclusions. We will emphasise that the review results need caution to avoid erroneous conclusions, acknowledging the potential impact of bias in the included studies. We will also provide a transparent explanation of why the sensitivity analysis was conducted and what it reveals about the robustness of the overall findings in the text. We will present the main results and key information regarding our assessment of the certainty of the evidence on the domains previously listed ( GRADEpro GDT ). The summary of findings table will include the review question, patient population, index test, target condition, reference standard, study quality, sensitivity, specificity, and likelihood ratios ( DTA Handbook 2023 ). We will use numbers and footnotes with explanations for our assessments. Two authors (ED and TT or AM) will independently perform the GRADE assessments and will then compare their assessments. In the event of discrepancies, and if a discussion does not help to reach an agreement, a third review author (CP) will be approached to settle the disagreements. We will follow this peer‐reviewed protocol during the review preparation and list any necessary deviations, providing reasons for the changes in 'Differences between protocol and review'. Assessment of reporting bias To reduce reporting bias, we will not use a search strategy filter, and we will not restrict our searches by language, date of publication, form of publication, or study size. We will not test for publication bias because of the lack of validated methods for diagnostic test accuracy reviews ( Leeflang 2014 ). Flow and timing Signalling questions and criteria Q1: " Was a consecutive or random sample of participants enroled? " Yes – If the study reports on a consecutive or a random selection of participants. No – if the study reports on another form of selection of participants. Unclear – if the study does not report on how the participants were enroled. Q2: Was a case‐control design avoided? Yes ‐ we will exclude case‐control study designs from this review. Therefore, we expect to classify all studies as 'Yes' for this signalling question. No – not applicable Unclear ‐ not applicable Q3: " Did the study avoid inappropriate exclusions ?" Yes – if definitions of exclusion criteria are appropriate (e.g. difficult to diagnose participants, failure at liver biopsy, failure on transient elastography with controlled attenuation parameters are not excluded inappropriately) and all exclusions are reported. No – if exclusion criteria are inappropriate and exclusions are not reported. Unclear – if the study does not report causes of exclusions. Q1: "Were the index test results interpreted without knowledge of the results of the reference standard?" Yes – if the study reports that the results of the index test were interpreted without the knowledge of the results of the reference standard or a prespecified threshold for abnormal levels of aspartate transaminase and platelet counts were used. No – if the study reports that results of the index test were interpreted with the results of the reference standard or threshold for abnormal levels of aspartate transaminase and platelet counts were changed after the reference standard results became available. Unclear – if the study does not report information about blinding of the results of the index test and reference standard, and it is not clear whether a prespecified threshold for abnormal levels of aspartate transaminase and platelet counts were used. Q1: " Is the reference standard likely to correctly classify the target condition? " Yes – if the study authors included only participants with liver biopsy that contained specimens of liver tissue with a length of at least 15 mm and at least 11 portal tracts that can provide reliable morphological staging of hepatic fibrosis and grading inflammation ( Rockey 2009 ). No – if the liver biopsy contained specimens of length < 15 mm or less than 11 portal tracts Unclear – if the study authors did not report the length of liver biopsy specimens and the number of portal tracts they contain. Q2: " Were the results of liver biopsy interpreted without knowledge of the results of APRI? " Yes – if the study reports that the results of the reference standard were interpreted without the knowledge of the results of the index test. No – if the study reports that the results of the reference standard were interpreted with the knowledge of the results of the index test. Unclear – if the study does not report information about blinding of the results of the reference standard and the index test. Q1: " Was there an appropriate interval between the index test and the reference standard? " Yes – if the index test and the reference were done within one day. No – if the interval was more than one day, but less than or equal to three months. Unclear – if the study does not report the interval between the index test and the reference standard. Such studies will be excluded from this review. Q2: " Did all participants receive the same reference standard (liver biopsy)? " Yes – Liver biopsy is the only reference standard that we accept for this review and is one of the inclusion criteria for this review. So, we expect to classify all studies as 'Yes' for this signalling question. No – not applicable. Unclear – not applicable Q3: Were all participants included in the analysis? Yes – if all enroled participants were included in the analysis. No – if any participant was excluded from the analysis for any reason. We do not expect this classification in any of the studies as these are routine blood tests which will be repeated in the rare case of technical failure. Unclear –if the exclusion of participants from the analysis is unclear. Risk of bias Could the selection of participants have introduced bias? Low risk: 'Yes' for all signalling questions. High risk: 'No' or 'Unclear' for ≥ 1 signalling question. Could the conduct or interpretation of the index test have introduced bias? Low risk: 'Yes' for all signalling questions. High risk: 'No' or 'Unclear' for ≥ 1 signalling question. Could the reference standard, its conduct, or its interpretation have introduced bias? Low risk: 'Yes' for all signalling questions. High risk: 'No' or 'Unclear' for ≥ 1 signalling question. Could the participant flow have introduced bias? Low risk: 'Yes' for all signalling questions. High risk: 'No' or 'Unclear' for ≥ 1 signalling question. Concerns about applicability Are there concerns that included participants and setting do not match the review question? Low concern: there was low concern that the included participants did not match the review question, i.e. an unselected group of people with chronic HCV infection without a previous diagnosis of fibrosis were included. High concern: there was high concern that the included participants did not match the review question. For example, people with chronic HCV infection with a high (or low) risk of fibrosis based on the results of other tests for liver fibrosis. Unclear concern: if it was unclear whether the participants included in the study matched the review question. Are there concerns that the index test, its conduct, or interpretation differ from the review question? Low concern: the index test, its conduct, or its interpretation does not differ from the way it is used in clinical practice (as defined in the Clinical Pathway section). High concern: the index test, its conduct, or its interpretation differs from the way it is used in clinical practice (as defined in the Clinical Pathway). Unclear concern: if it was unclear whether the conduct and interpretation of the index test differs from the way it is used in clinical practice (as defined in the Clinical Pathway). Are there concerns that the target condition as defined by the reference standard does not match the question? Low concern: Because of the inclusion criteria for this review, we expect only studies in which liver biopsy was performed and interpreted using standard criteria for the diagnosis of fibrosis. Therefore, we expect to classify all studies in the review as 'Low concern'. High concern: not applicable Unclear concern: not applicable. ‐ Appendix 2. documents.title: Psychotic Experiences and Risk of Suicidal Thoughts and Behaviors: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Population Studies.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND HYPOTHESIS: Since a prior systematic review and meta-analysis reported an association between psychotic experiences (PEs) and suicidal thoughts and behaviors, a large number of new studies have been published on the topic, including several novel studies on the association between PEs and transition from suicidal ideation to attempt.
STUDY DESIGN: Two authors independently searched PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, and PsycINFO databases from inception until July 2023, conducted data extraction, and assessed study quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa Quality Assessment Scale. Random-effects models were used to calculate pooled odds ratios (ORs) for the association of PEs and subsequent suicide ideation, suicide attempts, suicide death, and transition from suicidal ideation to attempt, first for the total population, and second stratified by age group. Secondary analyses assessed the mediating role of co-occurring psychopathology.
STUDY RESULTS: Twenty studies from 18 different samples (n = 81,861) were identified. Individuals who reported PEs had increased odds of subsequent suicidal ideation (k = 12, OR = 1.90, 95% CI = 1.65-2.19), suicide attempt (k = 13, OR = 2.95, 95% CI = 2.21-3.94), transition from suicidal ideation to suicide attempt (k = 3, OR = 2.83, 95% CI = 1.60-4.99), and suicide death (k = 1, OR = 4.39, 95% CI = 1.63-11.80). This heightened risk was stable across childhood, adolescence, and adulthood. PEs predicted suicide attempts over and above co-occurring psychopathology (k = 8, OR = 2.85, 95% CI = 2.06-3.95).
CONCLUSIONS: Individuals reporting PEs are at increased risk of all types of suicidal thoughts and behaviors. In addition, PEs are particularly important risk markers for future suicidal behaviors, including in individuals already reporting suicidal ideation. This risk is in excess of what is explained by co-occurring psychopathology.

This risk is in excess of what is explained by co-occurring psychopathology. suicidal ideation suicide attempt suicide ideation to attempt psychosis The Health Research Board ECSA-2020-005 Academy of Medical Sciences 10.13039/501100000691 APR8\1005 UK Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy pmc-status-qastatus 0 pmc-status-live yes pmc-status-embargo no pmc-status-released yes pmc-prop-open-access yes pmc-prop-olf no pmc-prop-manuscript no pmc-prop-legally-suppressed no pmc-prop-has-pdf yes pmc-prop-has-supplement yes pmc-prop-pdf-only no pmc-prop-suppress-copyright no pmc-prop-is-real-version no pmc-prop-is-scanned-article no pmc-prop-preprint no pmc-prop-in-epmc yes pmc-license-ref CC BY-NC Introduction Psychotic experiences (PEs) refer to hallucinations and delusions that typically occur at a sub-clinical level in the population. 1 PEs are significantly more common than psychotic disorders, 2 with a reported prevalence of 5%-7% in adults, 3 7.5% in adolescents, and 17% in children. 4 The psychopathological significance of PEs has been widely researched, and PEs are associated with a range of mental health difficulties. 5–7 In a previous systematic review, PEs were found to be associated with increased risk of suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, and suicide deaths. 8 Since the publication of that review, a large number of studies have been published on the association between PEs and suicidality, including several novel studies examining the association between PEs and transition from suicidal ideation to attempts. We conducted an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal studies looking at PEs and the risk of suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, and suicide death. We also looked, for the first time, at the relationship between PEs and risk of suicide attempt among individuals experiencing suicidal ideation (i.e., transition from suicidal ideation to attempt). Method Search Strategy We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, 9 of published longitudinal studies on PEs and their association with subsequent suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, transition from suicidal ideation to attempts, and suicide death ( Figure 1 ). The search strategy was based on a previous systematic review on this topic. 8 We searched the electronic databases PubMed, Excerpta Medica Database (Embase), Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), and PsycINFO from their inception until July 2023 for articles, with the following terms: psychotic experience, psychotic like experience, psychosis like experience, hallucinations, delusion*, psychotic like symptoms, and suicid*. We used the format “((‘psychotic experiences’[Title/Abstract] OR ‘psychotic-like experiences’[Title/Abstract] OR ‘psychotic like experiences’[Title/Abstract] OR ‘psychosis like experiences’[Title/Abstract] OR ‘psychosis-like experiences’[Title/Abstract] OR ‘hallucinations’[Title/Abstract] OR ‘Delusion*’[Title/Abstract] OR ‘psychotic-like symptoms’[Title/Abstract] OR ‘psychotic like symptoms’[Title/Abstract])) AND ((Suicid*[Title/Abstract]) OR suicide[Mesh]).” Records were imported into Covidence 10 and deduplicated. Figure 1. PRISMA Style Flow Diagram of Included Studies PRISMA flow diagram depicting the selection process of included studies. Three sections are shown: Identification, Screening, and Included. The Identification section shows previous studies and new studies identified via databases, registers, and other methods, with initial record counts and exclusions noted. The Screening section details record screening and eligibility assessments, including reasons for exclusions. The Included section lists the final number of studies and reports incorporated into the review, totaling 20 studies. Eligibility Criteria Inclusion criteria were: (1) an original, published article, (2) written in English, (3) about a general population sample, (4) involving prospective assessment of active suicidal ideation, transition from suicidal ideation to suicide attempt, suicide attempts (including interrupted or aborted attempts if applicable), or suicide death, and (5) with at least one follow-up point. Exclusion criteria were: (1) not longitudinal; (2) did not report odds, hazard, or risk ratios, or data that enabled the researchers to calculate these, and did not respond to requests for this information; and (3) only published as an abstract or conference summary. Study Selection and Data Extraction Screening of titles and abstracts, followed by full-text screening, was performed by two authors (K.O. and K.F.). Both authors independently extracted data on participants’ baseline age range, duration of follow-up period, PE and suicidality instruments, and suicidality outcomes ( Table 1 ). Any disagreements were resolved by consensus or discussion with a senior author (I.K.). Where necessary, authors of relevant studies were contacted to request additional information. Table 1. Study Quality The Newcastle-Ottawa Quality Assessment Scale was used to assess study quality, 11 based on 3 categories: selection, comparability, and outcome. High-quality was indicated by the exclusion of participants with baseline suicidal ideation or attempts (except for when analyses were examining the transition from suicidal ideation to attempt), employment of semi-structured interviews or validated self-report questionnaires, and the provision of raw, unadjusted data. The comparability category, which offers a maximum score of 2 for adjusting 2 variables identified as significant by the researchers, was deemed not applicable to the context of this review. Instead, a maximum score of 1 was offered if unadjusted odds ratios (ORs) or raw data to calculate these were available (including if these were provided by the study authors). Consequently, the scale was adapted to reduce the maximum score from 9 to 8, and a high-quality study was defined as scoring 6 or more. Two authors (K.O. and K.F.) independently completed the scale for each study and resolved disagreements by consensus. Initial disagreement (prior to consensus) between raters was 13.1%. The research article, supplementary material , and any additional information gathered from the authors of individual studies were all used for quality assessment. All included studies were rated high quality ( Supplementary Table 1 ). Statistical Analysis Unadjusted raw data was extracted to calculate ORs for the association of PEs with suicidal ideation, transition from suicidal ideation to suicide attempts, suicide attempts, and suicide deaths. When raw data were not available, ORs were used directly. Pooled results were calculated using a random-effect analysis, as heterogeneity was expected given differences in participant characteristics and methodology between studies. We used the τ 2 statistic to measure heterogeneity, this statistic represents the amount of between-study variance, with higher values indicating more variance, and significant values ( P < .05) indicating that it is likely there is significant between-study heterogeneity (i.e., differences in effect sizes are not due to sampling error alone). Publication bias was assessed using Egger’s test. Meta-analyses were conducted first for the entire sample, and second, stratified by the median age of participants at baseline report of PEs, as evidence suggests the PE and suicidality relationship may change across the lifespan. 12 Studies, were categorized into relating to either children (aged 12 years or younger), adolescents (aged between 13 to 18 years [inclusive]), or adulthood (aged over 18 years). In addition, a post-hoc meta-regression was conducted in the whole sample to test whether the association between PEs and suicidality was affected by age. Given variation in the mean follow-up duration reported by each study, a meta-regression was also conducted to determine whether the association between PEs and suicidality was affected by the length of follow-up period. Further, a secondary meta-analysis of studies that adjusted results for co-occurring psychopathology was conducted. Lastly, as several studies excluded participants with baseline suicidality, we also conducted a sensitivity analysis stratifying studies by whether baseline suicidality was excluded or not. Analyses were conducted using the meta package in R version 4.2.2. 13 Results Study Selection The literature search yielded 5,697 articles. Following removal of duplicates, we examined titles and, where necessary, abstracts to identify relevant articles. References to included studies were also reviewed. This process led to the identification of 69 studies for full text review. Fourty-nine studies were excluded, resulting in the inclusion of 20 articles ( Figure 1 ). The prior review on this topic 8 included 10 studies—nine of which were included in the current review, with one study excluded on the basis of not including a prospective suicidality measure. 14 Among the 20 included studies, 14 reported ORs, 15–28 4 hazard ratios, 29 , 30 and 4 relative risk. 31–34 To prevent redundancy, we excluded suicide attempt data from one 26 of two 26 , 34 studies reporting on the same data set with the same follow-up time. Similarly, from another pair of studies 18 , 19 with identical datasets and comparable follow-up durations, only one study that provided more comprehensive data 19 was used for analysis. We also included two sets of observations for one study 21 that presented data for two distinct age groups at different time points. These steps resulted in 12 studies reporting on suicidal ideation, 3 on the transition from suicidal ideation to suicide attempts, 14 on suicide attempts, and 1 on suicide deaths. Given the small numbers of studies reporting on the transition from suicidal ideation to suicide attempts and suicide deaths, these outcomes were not included in any secondary analyses. Of the studies on suicidal ideation, 5 reported results adjusted for co-occurring psychopathology, as did 8 on suicide attempts, with a large amount of variability in the type of psychopathology that was adjusted for (see Table 1 ). Sample Characteristics The 20 studies reported on a total of 81,861 participants from 18 samples and 11 countries (Australia, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Ireland, Mexico, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Sweden, the United Kingdom, United States). For 15 samples, information was reported on participant sex, and 33,789 (57.3%) of participants were female. The duration of the follow-up period varied between 1 month to 27 years, and baseline data from individual studies were obtained at the earliest in 1980, and at the latest in 2019. Nine studies 16 , 21 , 23 , 25–28 , 32 , 33 reported raw data on suicidal ideation. Suicidal ideation was reported by 10.3% of those sampled (3,179 of 30,759 individuals). Three studies 17 , 21 , 23 reported on the transition from suicidal ideation to attempts, documenting 55 instances among 9039 individuals (<0.1%). Regarding suicide attempts, 12 studies 16 , 17 , 19 , 21 , 22 , 24 , 27 , 28 , 31–34 found 851 instances among 32,923 individuals (2.6%). One study reported 24 suicide deaths in a sample of 15,049 individuals (<0.1%). 30 Meta-Analytical Results Suicidal Ideation Twelve studies reported on suicidal ideation (τ 2 = 0.03, P = .01). Egger’s test was non-significant ( t = −0.65, P = .53), and visual inspection of the funnel plot found no asymmetry ( Supplementary Figure 1 ), indicating a lack of publication bias. Discussion This updated systematic review and meta-analysis assessed the longitudinal association of PEs with suicidal thoughts and behaviors. Pooled results from 20 prospective cohort studies found that individuals who reported PEs had 2-fold increased odds of subsequent suicidal ideation, 3-fold increased odds of subsequent suicide attempt, and 4-fold increased odds of subsequent suicide death. In addition, PEs were associated with 3-fold increased odds of transition from suicidal ideation to attempt. We also found that analyses stratified for age showed a consistent association of PEs with the subsequent risk of suicidal ideation and attempts regardless of whether PEs were measured in childhood, adolescence, or adulthood. Lastly, we found a clearer relationship between PEs and more severe suicidal behavior (suicide attempts) than with suicidal ideation. The results of this meta-analysis confirm that PEs are associated with increased odds of suicidality across the full spectrum of severity of suicidal thoughts and behaviours. 8 , 35 The association between PEs and increased likelihood of transitioning to suicide attempt in individuals with suicidal ideation is a particularly important finding, as the majority of traditionally cited risk factors for suicide, such as depression, hopelessness, psychiatric disorder, and impulsivity, fail to differentiate between individuals who only experience suicidal thoughts and those who progress to attempting suicide. 36 That is, many factors considered to be correlates of suicide may actually only directly relate to suicidal ideation. This distinction is critical because most people who experience ideation do not go on to make a suicide attempt, meaning that factors that can differentiate those who attempt suicide from those who have ideation only are of key importance for suicide prediction and prevention efforts. 37 Our results indicate that PEs are one of the few risk factors that are associated with suicide attempts over and above suicidal ideation. However, only three studies reported on this relationship, and in each study the number of individuals reporting a transition from suicidal ideation to attempt was generally small. Further longitudinal research, particularly in clinical samples, to understand the potential utility of PEs as a marker for worsening suicide risk will be important. Adjustment for co-occurring psychopathology, (e.g., symptoms of anxiety and depression, or substance use disorders) did not explain the association between PEs and suicide attempts. This is consistent with previous cross-sectional research, 38 and with previous findings that PEs are not associated with suicidal ideation when individuals with suicide attempts are excluded, 39–41 suggesting that PEs are particularly important markers of more severe suicidal behavior. Interestingly, psychotic disorders have been associated with higher severity of suicide attempts and a greater intention to die in association with suicide attempts, in comparison to other types of psychiatric disorders. 42 , 43 Together with our findings that PEs predict the transition from suicidal ideation to attempts, this suggests that PEs are less clearly associated with suicidality in general but tend to be associated with greater severity of suicidality. However, there were fewer studies reporting on suicidal ideation than suicide attempts, and it is also feasible that the lack of association between PEs and suicidal ideation in adjusted associations reflects a lack of power to detect an effect. Our results also provide evidence that the PE-suicidality relationship is not specific to any developmental phase, but exists across the entire lifespan. Previous cross-sectional research has found that both the prevalence of hallucinations, and the association of PEs with suicidal ideation and behaviors decreases with older age. 12 This is consistent with accounts that PEs may be a normative part of childhood development, but become less normative and more indicative of psychopathology with age. 4 , 21 However, in the current study, we found that PEs were associated with increased odds of suicidal ideation and suicide attempts in childhood, adolescence, and adulthood, with little difference in effect sizes between the different age groups. This finding may be in part explained by the fact that only three studies examined the association between PEs and suicidality in adulthood, and all three examined an extremely broad age range (i.e., ~18 through to >65 years). This means that though we can confirm PEs are associated with suicidality in middle childhood and adolescence, we cannot rule out the possibility of differential effects in older age groups. Interestingly, we also found no effect of follow-up time on the relationship between PEs and suicidality, suggesting that as the relationship between PEs and suicidality is equally as strong in studies with short follow-up periods as long follow-up periods, PEs may act specifically as an acute marker of risk. Mechanisms underlying the association between PEs and suicidality are complex and are likely related to shared risk factors or developmental processes. PEs may directly cause psychological distress, which could lead to suicidality. Recent research, however, has shown that when children are asked to report how much distress they experienced specifically as the result of a PE, the amount of distress inherent to that PE mediated only a small portion of the relationship between that PE and both suicidal ideation and behavior. 44 Alternatively, the inverse relationship, where suicidal ideation and behaviors influence the development of PEs, could occur. This suicidal drive hypothesis posits that PEs are an externalized response to the self-directed threat of suicidal ideation or behavior. 45 However, evidence for this hypothesis from longitudinal studies has been inconsistent, with one study finding no reverse temporal link, 19 and another finding PEs exhibit a bidirectional relationship with suicidal ideation, with psychological distress acting as a shared risk factor. 46 While the current findings are associational and cannot be used to determine causality (nor the direction of causality), we note that PEs remain an important marker of risk for suicidality regardless of the mechanisms underlying the relationship. Shared risk factors, such as psychological, 47 environmental, 48 , 49 cognitive, 50 and biological factors, likely play an important role in understanding the association between PEs and suicidality, 8 with PEs acting as risk markers that capture important (suicidal behavior-related) aspects of these risk factors in the form of clinically measurable symptoms. There are a number of biological and psychosocial mechanisms that may underly the relationship. This includes factors like stigma surrounding PEs, 51–53 social isolation, 54–56 discrimination and racism, 57–59 all of which have been shown to be related to both PEs and suicidal ideation/behaviors. Furthermore, shared factors, include hopelessness, negative self-evaluation, emotional dysregulation, and trauma may mediate relationships between PEs and suicidality. 19 , 39 , 60 , 61 Further, we have hypothesized that PEs result from impaired efficiency of cooperation between different neural hubs involved in the coordination of complex mental processes, such as problem-solving, language, and social skills. 62 Deficits in these skills may become evident in the context of increased neural network demand resulting from increased psychological stress, which contributes to the development of suicidal behavior by, for example, reducing the efficiency of cooperation between neural hubs involved in language skills that allow one to effectively verbalize (and conceptualize) one’s challenges, hubs involved in complex social skills that facilitate effective social relationships and the eliciting of support from others, and hubs involved in complex problem solving. 62 Strengths and Limitations The major strength of this review was the use of longitudinal studies, which established a temporal association between PEs and suicidality. Further, studies captured a variety of age ranges, which allowed us to examine potential specific developmental effects. Limitations include that the vast majority of included studies were conducted in Europe, North America, and Oceania and may not reflect the true nature of the relationship between PEs and suicidality across the world; further research in other parts of the world, including the Global South, will be important. 63 The use of search terms in the English language only may have specifically contributed to this issue. There was heterogeneity in the measurement of suicidal ideation and attempts between studies; however, in general, studies reported relatively consistent findings on the association between PEs and suicidality. We examined associations adjusted for co-occurring psychopathology, but there was high variability in the type of psychopathology that was adjusted for, and most studies simultaneously adjusted for multiple variables, so it was not possible to draw conclusions regarding any individual factor. Further, most studies did not consistently adjust for other potential shared risk factors (e.g., environmental factors, cognitive factors), meaning we were unable to examine third variables outside of co-occurring psychopathology. These factors may be important in understanding the mechanisms that explain the relationship between PEs and suicidal behavior (explanatory models) but we note that they do not impact on the importance of PEs as a risk marker for suicidal behaviour (predictive models). Conclusion PEs are predictors of future suicidal thoughts and behaviors across age groups. The association of PEs with suicide attempts exists above and beyond the contribution of both co-occurring psychopathology and suicidal ideation, suggesting PEs are associated with increasing severity of suicidality. PEs also predict the transition from suicidal ideation to attempt. These findings underscore the significance of PEs as risk markers for suicidality and highlight the need for further causal research to understand the mechanisms underlying these relationships. documents.title: Differences in the effectiveness of individual-level smoking cessation interventions by socioeconomic status.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: People from lower socioeconomic groups are more likely to smoke and less likely to succeed in achieving abstinence, making tobacco smoking a leading driver of health inequalities. Contextual factors affecting subpopulations may moderate the efficacy of individual-level smoking cessation interventions. It is not known whether any intervention performs differently across socioeconomically-diverse populations and contexts.
OBJECTIVES: To assess whether the effects of individual-level smoking cessation interventions on combustible tobacco cigarette use differ by socioeconomic groups, and their potential impact on health equalities.
SEARCH METHODS: We searched the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews from inception to 1 May 2023 for Cochrane reviews investigating individual-level smoking cessation interventions. We selected studies included in these reviews that met our criteria. We contacted study authors to identify further eligible studies.
SELECTION CRITERIA: We included parallel, cluster or factorial randomised controlled trials (RCTs) investigating any individual-level smoking cessation intervention which encouraged complete cessation of combustible tobacco cigarette use compared to no intervention, placebo, or another intervention in adults. Studies must have assessed or reported smoking quit rates, split by any measure of socioeconomic status (SES) at longest follow-up (≥ six months), and been published in 2000 or later.
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: We followed standard Cochrane methods for screening, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment. We assessed the availability of smoking abstinence data by SES in lieu of selective reporting. The primary outcome was smoking cessation quit rates, split by lower and higher SES, at the longest follow-up (≥ six months). Where possible, we calculated ratios of odds ratios (ROR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for each study, comparing lower to higher SES. We pooled RORs by intervention type in random-effects meta-analyses, using the generic inverse-variance method. We subgrouped by type of SES indicator and economic classification of the study country. We summarised all evidence in effect direction plots and categorised the intervention impact on health equality as: positive (evidence that the relative effect of the intervention on quit rates was greater in lower rather than higher SES groups), possibly positive, neutral, possibly neutral, possibly negative, negative, no reported statistically significant difference, or unclear. We evaluated certainty using GRADE.
MAIN RESULTS: We included 77 studies (73 from high-income countries), representing 127,791 participants. We deemed 12 studies at low overall risk of bias, 13 at unclear risk, and the remaining 52 at high risk. Included studies investigated a range of pharmacological interventions, behavioural support, or combinations of these. Pharmacological interventions We found very low-certainty evidence for all the main pharmacological interventions compared to control. Evidence on cytisine (ROR 1.13, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.74; 1 study, 2472 participants) and nicotine electronic cigarettes (ROR 4.57, 95% CI 0.88 to 23.72; 1 study, 989 participants) compared to control indicated a greater relative effect of these interventions on quit rates in lower compared to higher SES groups, suggesting a possibly positive impact on health equality. CIs for both estimates included the possibility of no clinically important difference and of favouring higher SES groups. There was a lower relative effect of bupropion versus placebo on quit rates in lower compared to higher SES groups, indicating a possibly negative impact on health equality (ROR 0.05, 95% CI 0.00 to 1.00; from 1 of 2 studies, 354 participants; 1 study reported no difference); however, the CI included the possibility of no clinically important difference. We could not determine the intervention impact of combination or single-form nicotine replacement therapy on relative quit rates by SES. No studies on varenicline versus control were included. Behavioural interventions We found low-certainty evidence of lower quit rates in lower compared to higher SES groups for print-based self-help (ROR 0.85, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.38; 3 studies, 4440 participants) and text-messaging (ROR 0.76, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.23; from 3 of 4 studies, 5339 participants; 1 study reported no difference) versus control, indicating a possibly negative impact on health equality. CIs for both estimates included the possibility of no clinically important difference and of favouring lower SES groups. There was very low-certainty evidence of quit rates favouring higher SES groups for financial incentives compared to balanced intervention components. However, the CI included the possibility of no clinically important difference and of favouring lower SES groups (ROR 0.91, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.85; from 5 of 6 studies, 3018 participants; 1 study reported no difference). This indicates a possibly negative impact on health equality. There was very low-certainty evidence of no difference in quit rates by SES for face-to-face counselling compared to less intensive counselling, balanced components, or usual care. However, the CI included the possibility of favouring lower and higher SES groups (ROR 1.26, 95% CI 0.18 to 8.93; from 1 of 6 studies, 294 participants; 5 studies reported no difference), indicating a possibly neutral impact. We found very low-certainty evidence of a greater relative effect of telephone counselling (ROR 4.31, 95% CI 1.28 to 14.51; from 1 of 7 studies, 903 participants; 5 studies reported no difference, 1 unclear) and internet interventions (ROR 1.49, 95% CI 0.99 to 2.25; from 1 of 5 studies, 4613 participants; 4 studies reported no difference) versus control on quit rates in lower versus higher SES groups, suggesting a possibly positive impact on health equality. The CI for the internet intervention estimate included the possibility of no difference. Although the CI for the telephone counselling estimate only favoured lower SES groups, most studies narratively reported no clear evidence of interaction effects.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: Currently, there is no clear evidence to support the use of differential individual-level smoking cessation interventions for people from lower or higher SES groups, or that any one intervention would have an effect on health inequalities. This conclusion may change as further data become available. Many studies did not report sufficient data to be included in a meta-analysis, despite having tested the association of interest. Further RCTs should collect, analyse, and report quit rates by measures of SES, to inform intervention development and ensure recommended interventions do not exacerbate but help reduce health inequalities caused by smoking.
